entries.content:
### Reading and landing the work

```
hrn batch show 20260922-164137-1a216b     # the same table, during the run or after it
hrn batch diff 20260922-164137-1a216b alpha
hrn batch merge 20260922-164137-1a216b
```

`show` reprints the end-of-run table from the record; a batch still going shows its
tasks as `running` and says how many. The record is written before the first task and
renamed into place, so reading it mid-run gets a whole file, never half of one.

`diff` writes one task's changes to stdout and nothing else, so it pipes into `git
apply` or a pager: the commit against the base the batch branched from, or whatever is
still uncommitted in the worktree when the task never committed. Files git has never
seen cannot appear in a diff, so they are listed on stderr instead. A slot task that
committed nothing has an empty diff, and `diff` says it committed nothing: its slot has
gone back and may hold another task's work by now, or, when the task kept it (`slot <n>
kept`), `diff` says so and the work is still in it (`hrn ws list`).

`merge` merges the branches into whatever the repository has checked out, in spec
order, and never pushes. It takes every task that passed, or the ones you name; a task
that failed its gates is skipped even when named, so nothing unproven arrives by
accident. The tree must be clean first, since the merge would otherwise mix your work
with the agents'. At the first conflict it puts the tree back as it found it, says
which task, and stops — the branches are still there to merge by hand. `--squash`
records one commit per task, `<id>: <prompt>`, instead of a merge commit. Undo a whole
call with the printed `git reset --hard <commit>` command. It names the commit
from before the call and undoes every task merged in it, even if a later task conflicts.

`merge --rm` removes the worktree and branch of each task merged in that call,
including tasks merged before a later conflict; skipped and conflicting tasks stay.
It uses the same rules as `batch rm`: dirty worktrees stay and cause an error,
and slot tasks lose only their branch. The printed undo command names the commit
from before the merge; after removal, the task work is only in the reflog. If
removal fails for one task, the output counts only tasks whose worktree or branch
was removed.

`hrn batch rm <id>` removes what a batch made; the record and the run logs stay. For a
slot task that is only its branch `hrn/<id>`: the slot and its lease are not the batch's,
and stay. So is it for a task the record still shows waiting for a slot (hrn stopped
then), whose branch is made before the wait. It refuses while the branch is checked out in a worktree (a task still running).
For a fresh task it removes the worktree and the branch (it refuses a worktree with
uncommitted changes) when the record says the task made them (`branch_made`, set once
git made both, and dropped while a retry makes them again; a task whose record cannot say
so removes them at once, and one whose removal fails claims what is still there): a task that found them there
already, or that hrn left before it had them back, does not own them (they may be another
batch's), and they stay. Records from before the record's `ownership` field never said so:
there every fresh task's worktree goes, except one whose task failed before any attempt
with hrn's own "already exists; remove it or pick another task id" error. A directory git no longer counts as a worktree (on Windows a file
lock can leave one behind) is removed when it is empty and reported when it is not, and
its branch is deleted either way. One task that cannot be cleaned does not stop the
others.

entries.key: docs/batches.md > Batches and worktree cleanup > Clearing merged worktrees
entries.content:
## Clearing merged worktrees

```
hrn gc E:\work            # what would go, and why each worktree stays or goes
hrn gc --apply E:\work    # remove them
```

Worktrees outlive their pull requests: the session that made one rarely comes back, and with
a Rust `target/` or a `node_modules` inside, each can hold gigabytes. `hrn gc` looks at every
linked worktree of the repositories at PATH (a repository, any folder inside one, or a folder
whose repositories are found two levels down; configured roots or the current directory by default) and removes a
worktree only on proof that its work is merged:

When [automatic gc](commands.md#automatic-gc) is enabled, a successful batch merge also
checks the repository's batch-owned worktrees for the same proof of landing. A local merge
alone does not prove that the change reached the remote default branch.
Cleanup errors are warnings and do not change a successful merge's result; inspect the log
before undoing a merge whose worktrees may have been removed. MCP `batch_merge` behaves likewise.

- **On a branch:** GitHub (`gh pr list`) reports no open pull request for the branch, and one
  merged at the worktree's commit, or at a later commit that contains it, more than `--grace`
  ago (default 1h, so a session finishing up after its merge keeps its folder).
- **Made by an hrn batch** (a batch record names the folder): the batch has no task still
  running, and the worktree's commit is on the branch origin names as its default
  (`git ls-remote --symref`), fetched by name just before. A squashed or reworded landing
  is also recognised when the patch id of the task's whole diff, whitespace included but
  line numbers ignored, exactly matches one commit on that branch since their merge base.
  The comparison checks fewer than 2000 non-merge commits. If it reaches that bound or finds
  no exact match, a change that landed split over several commits, or inside a larger one,
  is still recognised when merging the task's commit into that branch is clean and leaves
  the branch's tree exactly as it is (`git merge-tree --write-tree`). A conflict, any
  difference, or a task whose own diff is empty keeps the worktree, so once the branch edits
  those lines again it stays. So does a `merge` attribute on any file the task or the branch
  changed since their merge base (a rename can move the merge to the other side's path), read
  from the branch's `.gitattributes` (and git's own attribute files) for the merge as well:
  a union or a custom merge driver can settle on the branch's side and make a merge look
  clean that dropped the task's change. For the same reason a `merge.default` setting keeps
  it. The branch's patch ids are read once per merge base in a run, streamed from `git log`
  so large binaries are not held in memory. Git older than 2.40 has no
  `patch-id --verbatim`, and the merge check needs Git 2.43 or later; a proof that cannot
  run keeps the worktree. With `--apply`, hrn deletes the task's
  branch with its worktree, including its own commits and messages; the change itself is
  on the default branch.

And only when nothing would be lost with it: the tree is clean (untracked files count), its
ignored files are build output (`target`, `node_modules`, `dist`, `.venv` and the like, or any
folder carrying `CACHEDIR.TAG`, with no repository and no link (symlink or junction) out of the
worktree inside, on every system, since git on Windows deletes through a junction; an ignored `.env` or notes keep it, because `git
worktree remove` deletes ignored files; its `.hrn/` may hold only the worktrees git lists there), it is
not locked (so a slot always stays, even one a batch record names), it holds no worktree that
stays and no separate repository (submodules are checked below), on Windows it has no junction
or directory symlink leading out of it anywhere in it (git deletes through those; on Linux and
macOS it unlinks a link, so a tracked `config -> ../shared/config` does not keep it, and a
tracked folder swapped for a link already shows as a change),
and the current directory is not inside it. Everything else stays and the listing says why: an open or
closed pull request, none at all, commits after the merged one, a detached `HEAD`, uncommitted
files. When `gh` fails (not installed, not logged in) or the fetch does, the worktrees that
needed it stay, and while any batch record cannot be read every worktree stays (it may be the
record of a batch still running). Main checkouts are never touched.

entries.content:
installed, not logged in) or the fetch does, the worktrees that needed it stay, and while any batch record cannot be read every worktree stays (it may be the record of a batch still running). Main checkouts are never touched.

The listing puts the removals first, with the size each one frees and the pull request's URL,
which is the record once the folder is gone. `--apply` checks each one again just before it goes
(its `HEAD`, branch, lock and files, ignored ones included) and leaves one that changed since the
scan, or that holds a worktree that stays, then removes it with `git worktree remove` (never
`--force`) and deletes the branch if it still points at the commit that was checked. git's
removal is not all-or-nothing: one that fails (a file held open on Windows) can leave part of the
folder deleted. Only merged, clean worktrees get that far. If git no longer lists the worktree
and its folder is empty or gone, hrn prunes git's entries, tries to remove the empty folder, and
deletes the branch; a handle that still prevents deleting the empty folder is reported.
Otherwise the branch stays. When git refuses removal because the worktree contains submodules,
hrn checks their trees recursively (including untracked and ignored files). Each submodule's
HEAD must match the commit its parent recorded, it must have no stash, and HEAD and local
branches must have no commits absent from its remote-tracking refs. Deinitialized submodules
keep the worktree because their repositories cannot be checked by this pass, and so does a
submodule repository with linked worktrees of its own (they would lose their repository). If
all checks pass, hrn moves the folder aside (a `.gc-*` sibling), prunes git's entries, deletes
the moved folder and the branch. A failed submodule check, or a folder that cannot be moved
(a file held open on Windows), keeps the worktree and branch whole; so does one git still
lists after the prune (locked meanwhile), which is moved back. A failure partway through
deleting the moved folder is reported with its path, which is left to delete by hand; the
worktree is no longer registered by then, so no later scan sees a half-deleted worktree.
A batch's record stays (`hrn runs prune` can drop
it once its worktrees are gone). Open pull requests are read on their own, so a long history
cannot hide one; with 1000 or more open, no worktree on a branch is removed. Up to 1000 pull
requests of every state are read besides; a branch whose pull request is older stays.

entries.content:
### Build caches

```
hrn gc --free-below 50G E:\work C:\Users\me\cargo-target
```

The same run looks for build caches: folders carrying a `CACHEDIR.TAG` with the convention's
signature, which Cargo writes into every target folder (pytest and ruff tag their caches the same
way), at each PATH and up to two levels down (a `.sec-target` beside its repository, each folder of
a `cargo-target` pool) and inside each worktree that stays, up to two levels down. A cache goes when no build holds it (Cargo keeps
`<profile>/.cargo-lock` locked while it builds: on Windows `LockFileEx` checks it, elsewhere
a non-blocking `flock` does) and nothing has written it for `--idle` (default 24h). Its last write is
the newest time among its profile folders (`debug`, `release`, one under a target triple), their
`deps`, `.fingerprint`, `build` and `incremental` folders, the files directly in a profile, and
anything the walk that sizes it sees inside. With `--free-below SIZE` (`50G`, `500M`), a drive with less
free than SIZE also loses its caches idle past `--min-idle` (default 2h), oldest first, until what
goes would put it above SIZE; free space is asked of the drive (`GetDiskFreeSpaceEx` on Windows,
`statfs` elsewhere), and a drive that cannot answer loses nothing more.
In scan reasons and the free-space report, drives are named by their mount point on Linux and macOS.
After `--apply`, each drive that was below SIZE in the scan reports its actual free space,
whether it reached SIZE or how far it remains below; the listing is still the full set of
removals for that run.

An idle Cargo cache inside a slot is trimmed instead: each profile's `incremental` directory is
removed. GC does not prune deps, fingerprints or build outputs individually because Cargo does not
touch reused artifacts, so their modification times do not identify the latest build's dependencies.
`--slot-cap` is off by default; when set, a cache above the cap is trimmed after `--min-idle` if its
incremental output is at least half the cap. If the cache would still exceed the cap after any
eligible trim, GC removes the whole cache instead; the next build in that slot rebuilds it.
`--free-below` also selects slot trims after `--min-idle` but does not itself remove a whole slot
cache. Dry runs report the removals and the bytes each trim would free. GC holds Cargo locks
while moving incremental folders aside and deleting them; leftovers are retried on the next run
without trimming a newer incremental folder unless it meets an idle, cap or free-space rule.

A cache stays when git tracks a file in it (a tagged test fixture is someone's), when it holds a
repository or a link leading out of it, when the current directory is inside it, or when its lock
cannot be checked. One inside a worktree that goes is not listed: the worktree's removal takes it.
The listing shows each cache's size, last build and verdict; `--apply` checks each one again just
before it goes (still tagged, nothing written since the scan, no lock held, nothing inside that must
stay), moves it aside to a sibling `.gc-<pid>-<unix nanos>-<name>` folder, probes its locks
again (including `flock` on Unix), then deletes its contents with `CACHEDIR.TAG` last. If a
build holds a moved cache's lock, it is moved back and kept. A failed move keeps the original
cache; a failed deletion leaves a tagged `.gc-*` folder for the next run. That leftover is
eligible regardless of `--idle`, after the other safety checks. A cache has no pull request to
stand as its record: the build that needs it again rebuilds it.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports
entries.content:
# Evaluations and reports

[← README](../README.md)

## Routing by evidence

`$HRN_HOME/route.json` (default `~/.hrn/route.json`) maps purpose categories to
`backend`, `model`, and `effort`. Each row also has `eval`, the source eval id
(absent for a hand-set row), and `set`, its date in `YYYY-MM-DD` form.
A missing file is an empty table; a malformed file is an error naming the file.
No initial table is supplied: the first evidence table follows a separately
approved hrn-evals run.

```sh
hrn route show
hrn route set implement -b codex -m sol --effort medium
hrn route from-eval <eval-id> --margin 0.05
```

`show` lists one row per purpose, sorted by category, or `(empty)`. `set` replaces
one row; any subset of backend, model and effort is accepted, with at least one
nonempty value. Backend names and effort levels use the usual run validation.
Purposes are review, debug, implement, refactor, test, research, plan, ops and unknown.
`from-eval` prints the proposed rows, then saves them, preserving existing rows
for purposes the eval did not measure. It reads saved results and calls no model.

For each purpose, task prompts are classified with the same rules as
`report --by purpose`. Pass rates sum that purpose's task results across repeats.
The margin is an absolute fraction from 0 to 1 (default 0.05): a best pass rate of
0.95 admits variants at 0.90 or above. Effort comes before model: first choose
the cheapest qualifying effort within each backend/model family, then compare
those winners by cost. Equal costs prefer plan-based claude or codex over api,
then lower effort, with variant names breaking remaining ties. Cost is the
variant's recorded median across the eval, since task rows do not store separate
costs. Variant choices inherit task and spec defaults as in the measured run;
evidence that mixes different choices within one purpose/variant is skipped.
The row carries the eval's id and date. Codex list-price estimates participate
in eval cost comparisons and routing through the same cost fields as api estimates.
Older records are not repriced.

`hrn run`, batch tasks (after inheriting spec options), and MCP `run` apply the
purpose's row only when backend, model **and** effort are all empty. The purpose is
the declared one (`--purpose`, the MCP `purpose` field, a batch task's `purpose`,
or a leading `Purpose: <category>` header), else the prompt's classified category.
Naming any of the three disables routing: routing never substitutes a named
model. Missing rows keep the existing backend default. An invalid row, whether it
names an unknown or disabled backend or an unknown effort, is skipped with a
warning on stderr and the run goes on unrouted; it never refuses the run.
Continued runs retain inherited choices, and the existing plan-limit switching
rules still apply. When a plan limit moves a routed run to the partner backend,
the routed model and effort are dropped and the run records no `routed_by`, so the
partner's results are not credited to the row. A batch attempt on any backend other
than the one its model and effort were chosen for (a limit switch or a retry) drops
them and `routed_by` the same way, whether they were routed or named.

The additive `routed_by` record field contains `category`, `declared` (true when
the purpose was declared rather than classified; omitted otherwise), `eval`
(absent for a manual row), and `set`. It is omitted for unrouted runs; older
records still load.
`hrn report --by routed` groups them as `<category> via <eval id>` or
`<category> via hand`, with unrouted runs under `-`, using the usual runs, ok,
and cost columns.

`hrn report` reads every run and batch record and prints three tables: runs, their tokens, and batches.

```

api         3   3 100%     48s          6       $0.42     $0.14    71%
all         9   8  89%     55s          8      ~$1.45     $0.15    90%

tokens by backend, since 2026-09-14 17:40 (7d)
backend  input  output  cache read  cache write  med context  peak context  from
claude   41.2k  210.4k        9.8M       610.3k        96.1k        212.0k  turns
api       3.1k   40.2k      870.0k        52.0k        48.5k         91.3k  mixed

batches by repository, since 2026-09-14 17:40 (7d)

~/src/example-app                1      3   100%             1      ~$1.03
```

entries.content:
52.0k 48.5k 91.3k mixed all 44.3k 250.6k 10.7M 662.3k 81.0k 212.0k mixed batches by repository, since 2026-09-14 17:40 (7d) repository batches tasks pass% med attempts total cost ~/src/example-app 1 3 100% 1 ~$1.03 all 1 3 100% 1 ~$1.03 ```

Runs group by backend, or by `--by model` (the model that answered), `--by dir` (the
workspace), `--by purpose` (what the run was for: review, debug, implement, refactor, test,
research, plan, ops or unknown) or `--by day` (the day the run started, on this computer's
calendar; days are listed in date order rather than largest first). The purpose is the one the run declared (`--purpose`, the MCP `purpose`
field, or a valid leading `Purpose: <category>` header); otherwise it comes from ordered keyword
rules on the prompt's first paragraph, or its second when the first matches no rule, with leading
`Label: value` lines skipped for an anchored instruction before trying the paragraph
as written, then with labels skipped as a fallback. A label's colon must be followed by a space or the
end of the line; URLs and Windows drive paths stay intact. A label's bracketed part and its
value are each kept to 600 characters, so a long note stays a label and a long value is not
cut short by its label. Each lead is lowercased
from a bounded prefix and capped at 600 bytes without splitting a UTF-8 rune.
Since a brief's later paragraphs mention every keyword, the first rule
that matches wins, and a prompt no rule matches (a vague one) is `unknown`. Columns: runs, how many ended `ok`, median duration, median turns, total and
median cost, and the cache share (cache-read tokens over every input token, cache writes included;
`-` when the backend reported no token counts). A `~` marks a list-price estimate
computed by hrn. The api and codex estimates come from the Claude table in
`internal/agent/api.go` and the OpenAI table in `internal/agent/prices_openai.go`.
Every cost hrn shows should be treated as an estimate, never a bill; other CLIs
may supply their own cost figures rather than use either hrn table. Codex uses
standard short-context prices, without service-tier or regional adjustments.
It also shows `-` when Codex usage is marked missing; Codex's and gemini's cache share divides
cache reads by input tokens that already include those reads.
Unknown costs are never summed as zero or included in the cost median. When no cost
is known, cost cells show `-`; otherwise the total counts runs without a known cost
(or batch tasks that ran without a known cost), for example `$1.23 (2 unknown)`. An explicitly
reported zero is known and shows `$0.00`. JSON rows include `runs_without_cost` or
`tasks_without_cost` when nonzero; older records without usage metadata retain a
known cost when it is positive.
Batches group by repository; their cost sums every attempt, passed or not. Runs without
a result (still running or killed), batches with a task still running, and records that
cannot be read are counted under the tables and left out of them.
The tokens table sums each group's input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens from the
runs' results. A run whose usage is missing has only partial counters, so it is left out of those
totals and counted beside the input total, for example `1.2k (1 unknown)`; the cells show `-` when
no run in the group has known usage, and JSON rows carry `runs_without_tokens` when nonzero.
The table also gives the median and peak context a model call carried (input including cache
reads and writes, counted once). Those come from a run's `usage` events when it has them (see
[Usage per turn](run-records.md#usage-per-turn)): every turn counts. A codex run or an older
record without them counts once, as its average, its totals over its turns, and its peak
is the larger of that average and its recorded last-call context. gemini records carry no turn
count, so a gemini run adds no context figure; its prompt count already includes its cached
tokens, which its cache share and totals count once, as codex's do. `from` says which: `turns`,
`totals`, `mixed`, or `-` when no run in the group reported tokens. In a `mixed` row the
median is over one average a run (a run with `usage` events gives the mean of its turns), so
per-turn values and per-run averages are never counted together; the peak is still the
largest of any run.
`--since` takes a window such as `7d`, `36h` or `90m`; `--json` prints the same rows as
JSON for scripts.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Reports > Weekly digest
entries.content:
### Weekly digest

`scripts/report-digest.sh` turns `hrn report` and the tool output shapes into one line of
JSON (see [Kept scripts](scripts.md)), so a week's runs can be compared with the last. Run
records stay on the machine that made them, where a hosted CI schedule cannot read them, so
schedule it there and append each week's line to a file. Cron starts `sh` with a minimal
`PATH`, so run it in a login shell:

```bash
0 8 * * 1 bash -lc 'cd /path/to/harness && bash scripts/report-digest.sh >> "$HOME/hrn-digest.jsonl" 2>&1'
```

On Windows, in PowerShell, name Git Bash by its path, since a plain `bash` may be WSL's:

```powershell
$a = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe' -Argument '-lc "cd /c/path/to/harness && bash scripts/report-digest.sh >> ~/hrn-digest.jsonl 2>&1"'
$t = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Monday -At 08:00
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'hrn weekly digest' -Action $a -Trigger $t
```

Both `hrn` and `go` must be on the login shell's `PATH` (or pass `--hrn` with a full
path). A failed week
appends its `{"error":...}` line instead, so a gap in the file is visible.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Measuring what shaping can touch
entries.content:
## Measuring what shaping can touch

Run `bash scripts/tool-shapes.sh --home /path/to/.hrn --days 30 --json` from the
repository root. `--home` defaults to `$HRN_HOME`, then `~/.hrn`; `--days` defaults
to 30 (a rolling window of 24-hour days), and JSON is the only output form.
It reads finished runs, including unsuccessful ones, started in that window.
The record envelope's `started` timestamp selects the window; flat records fall
back to the local timestamp in their run directory name. Unfinished runs are
excluded; unreadable finished records in the window are counted and excluded.

`shapes` classifies UTF-8 tool-result bytes as `test`, `log`, `json`, `table`,
`terminal`, or `other`, in that priority order. Tests have `go test`, `ok`, `FAIL`,
`=== RUN`, or `--- PASS|FAIL|SKIP|BENCH` lines, or are `go test -json` output
(every non-empty line an object with an `Action`); unified diff headers do not match.
Logs have timestamp or level prefixes; JSON must parse; CSV/TSV
needs at least two rows with a consistent field count. Shell results otherwise
count as terminal output. For unnamed results, a pending shell call (or a batch
entirely of shell calls) establishes that origin; mixed pending calls remain
`other` when their origin is ambiguous. The `claude` tables use only Claude runs
with recorded tool calls.

Each shape reports its fraction of all result bytes and an **estimate**:
bytes / 4 divided by input tokens from the same runs. Each run uses its `usage`
event sum when present, otherwise its `result.json` totals, otherwise no token
figure. Input includes `cache_read_tokens` for api and Claude; Codex's
`input_tokens` already includes cache reads, so those are not added again.
Cache writes are excluded. A missing denominator is `null`. All runs contribute
to `bytes` and `tool_result_share`; only runs with a token figure contribute bytes
to input-share estimates, including inline-script estimates. `runs.with_tokens`
reports that coverage beside `runs.with_usage` and `runs.read`. Existing estimates
count bytes once. `input_token_share_replayed_estimate` instead multiplies each
result's bytes / 4 by the number of later model calls and divides their sum by
the same input-token denominator. Later calls are the usage events
after the result when any are present; otherwise result ordinal `i` (starting at
1) and `result.json` total turns `n` give `max(0, n - i)`. The fallback approximates
calls as one-to-one with tool results; batches and calls without results can
break that assumption. Missing turns give zero later calls. Replay assumes the
text remains in context through the run's end. These are candidate byte budgets, not
measured savings or a strict bound on total context tokens.

`inline_scripts` lists the top 20 normalised command groups by count, with the
count, distinct run count, command bytes and label (`heredoc`, `python`, `node`,
`perl`, `go`). It recognises `<<`, Python `-c`, Node/Perl `-e`, and `go run` of
temporary Go files in `tmp`/`temp` directories or common temporary-directory
variables. Quoted strings, paths, numbers and identifiers longer than 12
characters become placeholders; whitespace collapses. `command` and `cmd`
input fields are supported; shell calls without either use the event's `text`
(including Codex command events). Normalisation is a heuristic, not proof that two
scripts are interchangeable. Totals cover all groups, including those beyond
20; repeated bytes include every occurrence of groups seen more than once,
even within one run. `inline_script_totals` gives each of the five labels, in
that order, its count, distinct run count and command bytes over all groups, so
a label whose groups never reach the top 20 still shows. Keeping a script still costs its invocation and result.
`inline_script_input_share_replayed_estimate` weights command bytes / 4 by
usage events after the command, or `max(0, n - i)` using its ordinal
among all tool calls when usage is absent, over the same token denominator.
`repeated_inline_script_input_share_replayed_estimate` applies that weighting
to every occurrence of groups seen more than once, including groups beyond 20.
The command fallback likewise approximates one tool call per model call.
Nothing from the records is quoted: no prompt, command, path, normalised form,
or output. The fixture home and Go tests exercise the measurement without model
calls. See [the local 30-day snapshot](tool-shapes.md) for the measured budgets.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Evals
entries.content:
## Evals

An eval is a batch with two more dimensions: a matrix of variants to compare and a
number of repeats. Every cell is an ordinary recorded run, scored by the same gates, so
the question "which backend, model and effort for this kind of task" gets an answer with
numbers behind it.

```json
{
  "parallel": 3, "mode": "yolo",
  "gate": ["go build ./... && go test ./..."],
  "matrix": [
    {"name": "opus-high", "backend": "api", "model": "claude-opus-5", "effort": "high"},
    {"name": "opus-low",  "backend": "api", "model": "claude-opus-5", "effort": "low"},
    {"name": "claude",    "backend": "claude"}
  ],
  "repeats": 3,
  "timeout": "20m", "max_cost_usd": 3,
  "tasks": [{"id": "vet", "prompt": "Run go vet and fix every finding."}]
}
```

A variant's `name` defaults to `backend[-model][-effort]`. Each cell becomes a batch
task with the id `<evalid>.<task>.<variant>.r<n>`, so branches from different evals never
collide. Retries are off for every cell on purpose: an eval measures what one attempt
does, and a retried attempt would score the harness rather than the backend. Everything
else, gates and mode and the budgets, `lean` and `compact_window`, carries through from the
spec; cells on claude and codex are lean unless the spec or task says `"lean": false` (see
[What a run loads](backends.md#what-a-run-loads)). `protect` carries through too,
but `protect_mode` defaults to `fail` in an eval: a cell that changed a file its gates rely
on did not earn its pass (see [Batches](batches.md#batches)).

A variant may set `"lean": true` or `"lean": false`, overriding the task and spec.
Omitting it preserves the task/spec setting and the lean default. A variant's
`lean` field is refused if any of its cells resolves to a backend other than `claude` or `codex`.
Give variants distinct names to compare lean within one eval, for example:

```json
"matrix": [
  {"name": "lean", "backend": "claude", "lean": true},
  {"name": "full", "backend": "claude", "lean": false}
]
```

Variants may set `retrieval` (`off`, `optional` or `required`) and
`retrieval_version`. An eval record may include `retrieval_manifest` and
`retrieval_comparison`: held-out tasks, coverage, preparation and online overhead,
and a gate. With equal success over complete comparable cells, the candidate passes
when its median model tokens over the pairs where both cells passed is lower by at
least the saving threshold: the larger of 10% and the baseline's own movement, the
range of its per-repeat passing medians over their mean (`baseline_median_movement`,
`saving_threshold`). A variant that fails cheaply is not efficient, and a saving
smaller than the baseline moves between repeats is noise. When the baseline passed in
fewer than two repeats the noise was not measured and there is no saving verdict. The
all-pairs medians stay in the record beside the passing ones. Failed attempts count in per-success usage;
zero successes leave that ratio null. The bundled synthetic fixture tests the
accounting and establishes no real model savings.

`hrn eval eval.json` prints what each variant did and how each task scored under it:

```
  variant                pass  attempts  median cost median time   turns   tools   context
  sonnet                   0%         1        $0.15         13s       2       1    101061
  haiku                  100%         1        $0.05         14s       2       1     71814

  task                     sonnet      haiku
  greet                       0/1        1/1
── eval cb867 · batch 20260922-164017-1bbd7c · 2 cells · 14s ──
```

That run is real: asked for a file containing exactly `hrn rocks`, Sonnet wrote `hrn rocks.`
and failed the gate while Haiku passed at a third of the cost. The run records are still
there to say why, which is the point of keeping them.

`tools` is the median number of tool calls, counted the same way on every backend; a run
that takes eight greps to read one file shows up here and not in `turns`. Under a variant,
a dim line gives the run statuses when any cell did not finish `ok`, and how many passes
changed nothing: right for "find the bug, if there is one", suspicious for "fix the
typos", how many cells committed on their own (the agent moved its branch or `HEAD` with git
itself, by a commit, reset or rename, which a prompt saying "do not run git" forbids;
recorded, not failed), how many cells have no known
cost, and when some cells failed, the passing
cells' median cost and context, since cheap failures pull the all-cells medians down.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Evals (part 2)
entries.content:
rename, which a prompt saying "do not run git" forbids; recorded, not failed), how many cells have no known cost, and when some cells failed, the passing cells' median cost and context, since cheap failures pull the all-cells medians down.

A failed cell whose run ended `ok` in one turn, with no tool call and no change, *did not
act*: an agent that answered "I can't access the files" or that misread the task's own
instructions measured the eval's setup, not the variant. Such cells are counted apart
(`did not act` under the variant, `+1 did not act` after a task's score), left out of the
pass rate and the medians, and the footer says to re-run them; `hrn eval diff` notes a side
that has them, and the routing table built from an eval and `hrn eval list` count the
same way. A task whose deliverable is the answer (an `expect` and no gate) is the
exception: there the answer is the work, so a wrong one is a failure.

A cell *did not start* when every one of its attempts records `did_not_start`: the
run ended `error` with an error and no sign that a model was reached (no turns, tool
calls, final answer or tokens; some adapters never count turns, so tokens decide).
The reason is the first line of that error, such as a missing CLI, a refused launch
or an unsupported resume or option. A gate that could not start is a gate failure,
not a start failure: the agent ran before it. A cell with one attempt that ran and
failed and a retry that never started is a failure. These cells are counted
separately on variant and task rows, beside `did not act`, and in `hrn eval diff`.
Both counts are excluded from pass-rate denominators and medians, including in
`hrn eval list`; the status histogram and total cell count still include them.
Any turn or tool call rules out this classification. Short duration alone,
timeouts, cancellations, an ordinary failing gate, and a successful idle answer
are not evidence of a failed start. Old records without the field retain their
previous classification. Batch retries are unchanged.

After every first-round cell finishes, `rerun_unstarted` gives cells whose every
attempt did not start extra rounds. An omitted JSON field defaults to 1; `0`
disables reruns and negative values are refused. A Go caller constructing a `Spec`
sets `RerunUnstarted` explicitly (its zero value disables reruns). Each round runs
only cells still unstarted, through the same batch path, on the same base commit
with the original prompt, backend, model and options. Each gets a fresh task id
with `.u<round>` appended, such as `e.task.variant.r1.u1`. A cell that started is
never rerun, even when it failed. Cancellation or a batch infrastructure error
stops further rounds.

The eval record's `results` retains every first-round `TaskResult` followed by
every rerun result, including all attempts, diagnostics, tokens and timing.
The first rerun that starts replaces the original for scoring, whether it passes
or fails; unsuccessful launches remain in the record. The backing `batch_id`
identifies the first batch; extra rounds also have their ordinary batch records, listed in `rerun_batch_ids`; with `--keep`, `hrn eval` prints a `hrn batch rm` for each.
All known attempt costs, including unsuccessful launches and reruns, count in
`total_cost_usd` and eval totals. Performance medians use the selected result.

Variant and task rows record `reruns` (distinct cells given an extra round, not
the number of rounds) and `reruns_exhausted` (rerun cells still unstarted after
all configured rounds). Zero counts are omitted. Scheduled cells remain the
sum of first-round cells: variant `attempts` and task `total` never grow with
reruns. `did_not_start` counts cells still unstarted after reruns; pass rate is
`passed / (scheduled - did_not_start - did_not_act)`, or zero when none acted.
Variant `start_rate` (`BackendStartRate` in Go) measures first-round started
cells / scheduled cells, or zero with no cells. It stays below 100% after a
recovered launch, so recovery cannot hide launch reliability. The table and
`hrn eval diff` show start rate beside the did-not-start and rerun counts.
Old rows without `start_rate` derive it from their original `attempts` and
`did_not_start`; their pass rates are unchanged, and absent rerun counts are zero.

As in `hrn report`, an unknown cost (a
codex cell marked missing, a cell with no attempt) is never counted as zero: the median
cost and `total_cost_usd` cover the known costs, `cells_without_cost` counts the rest,
`median cost` is `-` only when no cell's cost is known, and a known zero shows `$0.00`.

entries.content:

The record goes to `~/.hrn/evals/<id>.json`; `--json` prints it, `hrn eval show <id>`
reprints it, `hrn eval list` finds it, `-v` streams every agent's tool calls. The worktrees are removed once the
record is safely written, unless `--keep`. A failing variant is data, not an error, so
the exit status is 0 when cells ran, even if they failed their gates. If no cell
could start because its provider was unavailable, it exits non-zero and names the provider.

Task ids and variant names take letters, digits, `_` and `-`: dots separate the parts of
a cell id. `retry` is refused in an eval spec, because a retried cell would score the
harness rather than the backend, and for the same reason an eval sets `no_switch`: a cell
whose backend reaches its usage limit ends `limited`. The `context` column counts prompt tokens and cache
reads together, which is what the model was given rather than what was billed at full
rate.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Evals > Harness variants
entries.content:
### Harness variants

A variant can also change the harness around the model, so a reworded brief, a new rule
or a skills set is scored by the same gates as a model change:

- `prompt_prefix` goes before every task's prompt, separated by a blank line, on every
  backend. The judge still grades against the task's own prompt.
- `append_system_prompt` is added after the backend's own system prompt: a rule, or tool
  guidance. The api backend sends it as its own system block (cached with the rest);
  claude gets `--append-system-prompt`. At most 16 KiB.
- `no_skills: true` starts the claude CLI with its skills off (`--disable-slash-commands`),
  to measure what they add. A lean cell already runs without skills, so the spec or task
  sets `"skills": true` (or `"lean": false`) for the comparison; `no_skills` on a lean
  claude cell without them is refused.

```json
"skills": true,
"matrix": [
  {"name": "base",  "backend": "claude"},
  {"name": "rule",  "backend": "claude", "append_system_prompt": "Run the tests before you answer."},
  {"name": "brief", "backend": "claude", "prompt_prefix": "Read the failing test first."},
  {"name": "bare",  "backend": "claude", "no_skills": true}
]
```

As with `lean`, a cell whose backend would ignore the field is refused before anything
runs: `append_system_prompt` on anything but `api` and `claude`, `no_skills` on anything
but `claude`. The check covers the value a cell ends up with, whether the variant, the
task or the spec set it. The two run options work outside an eval too (`hrn run
--append-system-prompt`, `--no-skills`, a batch spec, the MCP `run` tool); there, a backend
that cannot apply them says `not enforced`. The claude CLI is refused the system prompt
when it is installed as an npm `.cmd` shim, since `cmd.exe` would read the text as
commands; the native `claude.exe` takes it.

A route row holds only a backend, model and effort, so `hrn route from-eval` skips harness
variants (and tasks or specs that set the two run options): their score would be credited to
the model and routed without the change. A retrieval comparison refuses them for the same
reason.
Routing also skips cells with non-default `lean`, `shape_tools` or `retrieval` settings;
lean affects only claude and codex cells. Each skipped cell is printed with its task,
variant and reason; retrieval comparisons require matching variant `lean` and
`shape_tools` settings.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Evals > The judge
entries.content:
### The judge

Gates prove the build and `expect` proves an answer; neither can tell a typo fix from a
spelling change. A `judge` reads each passing cell's diff against a rubric and scores it
from 0 to 10:

```json
"judge": {
  "backend": "claude", "model": "haiku",
  "rubric": "Only real misspellings are fixed. British spellings such as colour stay.",
  "rubrics": {"notes": "The answer is correct and the repository is unchanged."}
}
```

`rubric` applies to every task and `rubrics` replaces it for the tasks it names; every
task needs one or the other, and both are checked before any agent starts. The judge is
shown the task, the rubric, the agent's final answer and the diff (the first 60 KB, and
the names of untracked files), and runs read-only in a copy of the cell's files so it can
open a file the diff only touches. The judge is blind to the variant: the prompt never
names it, and the copy is a fresh repository in a temporary directory named
`hrn-judge-<random>` holding two commits on branch `candidate`: `base` (where the eval
started) and `candidate` (the cell's files), so `git diff HEAD~1` shows the whole change
past the 60 KB the prompt holds. Neither its path, its branch nor its history says which
variant made the change (the cell's own worktree and branch do). A cell's copy is
removed once its last verdict is in. Each verdict's agent gets a fresh temporary
`HRN_HOME`, removed after the run, so it does not see the real home's run records through
that environment variable. Hrn still saves the judge's own run record in the real home.
This is not complete isolation: worktree directory names under the repository's `.hrn`
can still be read through the repository and may reveal variants, and read-only mode does not
limit reads, so a judge that opens the real home by its path (`~/.hrn` or the `HRN_HOME` value)
can still read run records.
Verdicts are asked for in a shuffled order seeded by the batch id, not variant by
variant. `backend` defaults to the default backend, `timeout` to 5
minutes per verdict. Cells that failed are not judged: they already scored where it
counts, and judging them would only spend money.

The scores join the table as a `judge` column per variant (the mean) and after each
task's pass count (`1/1 10.0`). Every verdict is in the record under `judgements`, with
its reason and the run id of the judge's own recorded run; a judge that fails or answers
without a `{"score": ...}` object is recorded as an error rather than a zero, and the
footer counts those.

A judge is a model, and it may not give the same diff the same score twice. `"repeats": 3`
in the judge scores every passing cell three times, on the same prompt (the diff and the
answer are read once per cell), each verdict its own run with its `repeat` number in
`judgements`. The mean then covers every verdict, and a `spread` column shows the lowest
and highest mean of a single repeat, over the cells scored in every repeat (a verdict that
failed in one repeat would otherwise move that mean by the cell's difficulty): how far the
variant's score moves when only the judge runs again. Task rows show it too (`2/2 7.5 (7.0-8.0)`), and the footer says `(3 per cell)`.
Repeats multiply the judge's cost, not the agents'; the default is 1. On the `claude` backend the first verdicts cost more than the
answer: Claude Code writes its own system prompt to the cache in the read-only mode the
judge uses, about 64k tokens, once per judge that starts before the cache exists.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Evals > Comparing evals
entries.content:
### Comparing evals

The records are kept so a change can be scored: run the same task set before and after
a new model, a reworded prompt or a harness change, then `hrn eval diff <before> <after>`.
Variants are matched by name and tasks by id; every cell reads before → after, and a
variant only one side ran gets its own row instead of disappearing. When a task's prompt
differs between the two specs, a note says so: often that is the change being measured,
but those rows do not compare like with like.

```
  eval cb867 → 847f6

  variant              pass             median cost        median time
  sonnet               0% → 100%        $0.15 → $0.14      13s → 13s
  haiku                100% → 100%      $0.05 → $0.05      14s → 16s

  task                 variant              passed
  greet                sonnet               0/1 → 1/1
  greet                haiku                1/1 → 1/1
  note: the prompt differs for task greet, so its rows compare different tasks
```

That is the greeting eval from above, run again with the target line fenced in
backticks. The first prompt ended "containing exactly the line: hx rocks. Do not run
git.", and Sonnet took the sentence's full stop as part of the line; with the text fenced
it passed. A judge score column appears when either eval was judged; `--json` prints the
pairs as data.

When either side's judge ran with repeats, the score shows its spread (`8.0 (7.0-9.0) →
8.5`), and a change smaller than the larger of the two spreads is marked `(within noise)`
(`within_noise` in `--json`), on variant and task rows alike: the judge disagreed with
itself by more than that. With no repeats on either side there is no spread to compare
and nothing is marked. A different number of judge repeats does not count as a changed
judge; a variant that changes its backend, model, effort, `prompt_prefix`,
`append_system_prompt`, `no_skills`, `lean`, `shape_tools`, `retrieval` or
`retrieval_version` under the same name gets a note.
The diff also notes changes to a shared task's effective `backend` and run options,
including values inherited from the spec,
except `shape_tools`, which the variant always overrides. These options are `model`,
`mode`, `max_turns`, `effort`, `mcp`, `no_instructions`, `no_context_edits`, `lean`,
`skills`, `append_system_prompt`, `no_skills`, `compact_window`, `allow_dangerous`,
`inherit_env`, `timeout`, `max_cost_usd`, `task_budget`, `no_switch`, `issue`,
`take_over`, `retrieval`, `retrieval_tenant`, `retrieval_project`,
`retrieval_revision` and `retrieval_version`. They appear as `task_options_changed`
in JSON, even when a variant overrides the task setting.

Every run records the agent setup it started with ([run records](run-records.md)): the
instruction files its backend loads, its MCP servers, plugins and skills, and its harness
options. When a variant's runs started with a different setup on the two sides beyond the
variant's own options (`base_digest` differs), the diff says so and names what differs, so
a score moved by an unrelated AGENTS.md, rule or skill edit is not credited to the change
under test:

```
  note: variant base started with another agent setup in 847f6, beyond its variant fields: files .claude/rules/tests.md; skills check
  note: variant base's cells in cb867 did not all start with the same agent setup
```

The second note means repeats of one task on that side started with setups that differ
beyond their options, so its row already mixes setups. The comparison uses the first cell
of each spec's first task, and only when both specs start with the same task: tasks may set
their own MCP configs. A variant that changed its backend, whether the variant, the spec, a
task or the default backend changed it, loads other files by design and gets only the
variant note. When the first task's run is gone, or the eval is older than the field, there
is no setup to compare and no note. `setup_changed` in `--json` lists the same.

entries.key: docs/evaluations.md > Evaluations and reports > Evals > Comparing a setup change
entries.content:
### Comparing a setup change

A branch that edits AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, rules or skills changes how every later task
runs, and review cannot see whether that helped. `hrn eval setup` measures it: it runs the
spec's one variant twice on the branch's code, once with the base's setup files and once
with the branch's own, and compares the two cell by cell.

```
hrn eval setup --base origin/main --held-out 0.5 --seed 7 setup-eval.json
```

The baseline runs on a commit hrn makes on top of `HEAD` whose setup files are as they were
where the branch left `--base` (their merge base, so setup edits made on `main` since do not
count as the branch's): every `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `HRN.md` in the tree and
everything under `.claude`, or the git pathspecs `--paths` names, comma-separated. Nothing is checked out for it and the
checkout is left alone; when those files are the same on both sides there is nothing to
compare and it refuses. Both sides then run as ordinary evals with the same tasks, gates
and budgets, and the candidate's record holds the comparison under `setup_comparison`.
The spec needs exactly one variant, on a plan backend named in it (`claude` or `codex`),
since every task runs twice, and at least two repeats. `--held-out 0.5 --seed 7` runs half
the tasks of each purpose, picked in an order the seed fixes, so a later comparison can run
on the same ones; the record keeps the task ids, the share and the seed. Both batches'
worktrees are removed when it ends, also after an error, unless `--keep`; `--json` prints
only the comparison on standard output, with the progress on standard error, and
`-v` streams every agent's tool calls.

The verdict is `better`, `worse`, `same` or `inconclusive`. Cells are compared in pairs of
the same task and repeat: when either cell of a pair never acted, or a cell ran on one side
only, the pair is left out of both sides (the reason counts them, and says to re-run the
cells that did not act), so a setup
that makes the agent give up on a hard task cannot drop that task from one side only. A pass rate counts as higher or lower
only when the difference is larger than the baseline's own pass rate moves between repeats.
With the same pass rate, the token saving is read over pairs of the same task and repeat
where both cells passed (reported counts only, not estimates), and must reach the larger of
10% and the baseline's passing median's own movement between repeats; a cost that grows by
as much is `worse`. When the baseline passed in fewer than two repeats that movement was not
measured, and with fewer than two pairs passing on both sides there is too little to compare:
both are `inconclusive`. Each side also reports the tokens its failures spent and its tokens per
success. A judge's scores, when the spec has one, appear in the diff printed above the
verdict and never change it: the gates decide passing.

# Backends and continuing runs

[← README](../README.md)

## Backends

The status column preserves the original implementation notes. It is not a current
compatibility matrix for every CLI version; check your installed backend with `hrn backends`.

| Backend | Billing | How it runs | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `api` | per token | The harness's own loop: Messages API (streaming, adaptive thinking, prompt caching, server-side refusal fallbacks on `claude-opus-5`) + [built-in tools](permissions.md#api-tools) + MCP tools. Needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or an OAuth `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`); `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` overrides the endpoint. | Every path is covered by tests against a fake API server; it has not yet run against the real API. |
| `claude` | your Claude subscription | `claude -p --output-format stream-json`. Found on PATH, `~/.local/bin`, npm, or the Claude desktop app's bundled build (that build needs its own `claude /login` first). | Verified end to end: `run`, `batch`, `eval`, and Claude Code delegating through `hrn mcp`. |
| `codex` | your ChatGPT subscription | `codex exec --json`. Found on PATH, npm, or the Codex desktop app's bundled build. | `run` and `--continue` (fork, and handing a claude run over) verified on codex-cli 0.155; not exercised by `batch` or `eval`. |
| `gemini` | your Google login | `gemini -o json` (single JSON result, no live stream). | Not yet run for real. |
| `opencode` | whatever opencode is configured with | `opencode run --format json`, prompt attached as a file. | `run` verified; not exercised by the later layers. |
| `agy` | your Antigravity plan (Google) | `agy --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json`, the prompt as one stream-json event on stdin. Found on PATH or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\agy\bin` (Windows), or `~/.local/bin` elsewhere. | Parser tested against an anonymised agy 1.3.3 sample; `run` and `--continue` verified once each on agy 1.3.3 (2026-10-14); not exercised by `batch` or `eval`. |

"Verified" means a real agent did real work through that path and the result was checked
by hand, not that a test passed. Treat the unverified rows as drafts that need one run and
probably one fix.

Without preferences, the default backend is `api` when credentials exist, otherwise
`claude`, or the route table's row for the prompt's purpose, when one exists.

entries.key: docs/backends.md > Backends and continuing runs > Backends > Choosing which backends hrn may use
entries.content:
### Choosing which backends hrn may use

The [Backends card in hrn watch](watch.md#backends) can also change the enabled backends and default.

Set the enabled backends once for runs, MCP calls, batches, eval cells and judges,
and the supervisor protocol:

```bash
hrn backends set --only claude,codex --default claude
hrn backends
hrn backends reset
```

`set` validates names against the backends registered in this hrn binary and writes
`$HRN_HOME/backends.json` (normally `~/.hrn/backends.json`) atomically:

```json
{"enabled":["claude","codex"],"default":"claude"}
```

For a build that registers `agy`, use `--only claude,agy` instead. A name need not
be installed to be enabled, but it must be registered. `--default` is optional;
when supplied it must appear in `--only`. `set` replaces the backend preference while keeping the work map keys.
`reset` keeps the work map keys and restores today's default
selection. A missing file or an empty enabled list with no default leaves all
backends enabled. A nonempty default without an enabled list is refused.

The same file accepts `work_map_repos`, `work_map_github` and `work_map_sessions` for the
[work map](work-map.md); GitHub collection and session collection default to enabled.

The configured default wins when installed; otherwise hrn chooses enabled `api`
when credentials exist, then the first installed enabled backend in preference
order. When none is installed it names the configured default, or else the first
enabled backend, so the run fails because that backend is not installed. Without
preferences the fallback is `claude`. `hrn backends` shows enabled/disabled, the
configured default (or the selected default when none is configured), availability
and remembered limits beside each backend. The MCP `backends` tool marks one default:
the backend a run without `backend` would use.

An explicit disabled backend is refused before execution (`hrn run` exits 2). So is
`hrn run --continue <id>` without `-b` when that run's backend is now disabled; the
refusal comes before a prompt is read from stdin.
Purpose routing ignores disabled rows with a warning and records no routing evidence;
`hrn route set` with a disabled backend saves the row and warns that runs ignore it.
Batch retry lists lose disabled entries while keeping their original order and
repetitions; a nonempty list with no enabled entries is refused.

At a usage limit the carry-on partner is the first other installed enabled backend
in preference order that passes the readiness and billing checks: one that is limited
too, or would bill per token, is passed over for the next. With no preference, the
claude/codex pairing is unchanged. With no ready enabled partner, the run stays limited.
Automatic carry-on partners are limited to claude, codex and agy; gemini and opencode can still be run by name.
An opted-in local api endpoint comes after all of them (see
[A local model as the last partner](#a-local-model-as-the-last-partner)).
`--no-switch` still disables carry-on. A limited run with
retrieval on is not carried on when its chain's latest retrieval pin was recorded on
another backend than the partner (usually the limited one): the partner would resolve
a new knowledge version, so the run stays limited and hrn prints the refusal, naming
the pinned run and version (see
[Continuing a run](#continuing-a-run)).

Agy runs with `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, and `GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI` withheld, including with `--allow-dangerous` and `--inherit-env`, so it uses its plan login. The run names any it withheld (never the value).

The `agy` adapter sends one `{"event":"user","message":{"content":"..."}}` line on
stdin with `--input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json`, which selects
print mode without putting a long prompt in Windows' command line. The `antigravity`
IDE launcher is not the CLI. `-m` passes `--model` (use `agy models` to list IDs), and
all hrn effort levels pass through as `--effort`: low, medium, high, xhigh and max.
Usage comes from the result event; output tokens already include thinking tokens,
and input tokens exclude cache reads. When agy exits 0 without a result event (a
truncated stream), the run stays `ok` with the answer it streamed, its usage is marked
`missing`, and an info line says no result arrived; the counters are what the finished
(`DONE`) steps reported, if any, never an estimate. A requested model is retained, but marked as
reported only if an event names one.

| hrn mode | agy flags |
|---|---|
| `readonly` | `--mode plan` |
| `ask` | `--mode plan` (no interactive approval) |
| `auto` | `--mode accept-edits` |
| `yolo` | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` |

These are agy's permission modes; `plan` is not a filesystem sandbox.

The `claude` backend uses the plan login only. If Claude Code's init line reports an
`apiKeySource` other than `none`, hrn stops the worker as soon as that init line arrives
and ends the run with an error. Claude Code may already have sent its first request.
Older CLI versions that omit the field keep their existing behaviour.

entries.key: docs/backends.md > Backends and continuing runs > Backends > Context management
entries.content:
### Context management

A long run carries every tool result, and the cap is 30 KB per result, so the
conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens. The api backend therefore asks
the server to clear old tool results itself (`clear_tool_uses_20250919`). hrn still
uploads its whole history, which stays append-only; what the clearing changes is the
context the model is given, so it is the context window and the billed input that
shrink, not the request body. A clear invalidates the cached prefix from that point,
which is the trade: one cold turn for a smaller context afterwards. That balance has
not yet been measured against a real long run, so compare `cache_read_tokens` across
two runs before trusting it. If the API ever refuses the beta, the run says so and
retries once without it. `hrn run --no-context-edits` turns it off for good, as do the
`no_context_edits` field on a batch spec or task and the MCP `run` argument.

`hrn run --mask-tool-results N` (batch/MCP `mask_tool_results`) opts into request-only
masking for endpoints without server clearing; 0 is off and negative values are rejected.
It replaces server clearing, even without `no_context_edits`. Once there are at least
2N tool results, older results are replaced in steps of N by one-line notes, leaving
between N and 2N-1 newest results whole. Results of at most 256 bytes also stay whole.
Notes retain the tool summary, byte count and any `read_original` handle. Stored history,
`messages.json`, durable checkpoints and run events keep the full results. This option
has only been tested against the fake server.

Whatever the server reports about the edits it applied is recorded as an info event,
`server context management, turn N: {...}`, with the JSON exactly as it arrived: its
shape was not documented where this was written, so hrn keeps it rather than guessing at
it. Nothing about it goes back into the history.

Claude Code version and whether each run follows the instruction.

Measured on 2026-10-13, when lean meant `--strict-mcp-config` alone (Claude Code 2.1.284, claude-sonnet-5-5, a developer's own setup, one

| Run | `context_tokens` | `cache_read_tokens` | `cache_write_tokens` | Turns |

| lean | 55,150 | 92,042 | 17,997 | 2 |
