When a continuation carries a saved session or conversation with more than 150,000 tokens
of context, the new run records the fresh-run warning once as an `info` event on every
entry path (CLI, MCP and exec). It appears in `hrn show` and the run page like other info
events. Passing earlier turns only as a transcript does not produce this warning.

Beside `runs/`, `limits.json` holds the reset time of each backend whose usage limit is in
force. `hrn run`, the MCP `run` tool and batch attempts consult it before starting when
switching is enabled. `hrn exec` neither reads nor writes it. Deleting it forgets the
remembered limits.

`result.json` includes `model_reported: true` only when the backend reports its
model: api responses, claude init lines, gemini model stats and codex's session
file. A requested/default model alone does not set it; opencode does not report one.
The field is omitted when false, and older records without it still load. Exec uses
it to send an empty `resolved_model` when the backend did not report its model.

`codex exec --json` names neither the model nor the CLI version, so after the run hrn
reads the session's rollout file, `$CODEX_HOME/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*-<session>.jsonl`
(default `~/.codex`): the last `turn_context` model becomes `model` with
`model_reported: true` (and prices the cost estimate), and `session_meta.cli_version`
becomes `result.cli_version`. Without that file, or when its `session_meta` names
another session, the result keeps the requested model, unreported, and no
`cli_version`. hrn never reads `config.toml` for this: it says what codex would use,
not what it ran.

When complete events fail to write or `events.jsonl` fails to close, `result.json`
includes `record_error` with the number of events not recorded, the first event error
and any close error; `hrn show` and MCP `show` report it and recover intact events
after broken lines. The result is still saved to mark the run finished, the field is
omitted on success, and older records still load.

`hrn runs prune --older-than 30d` removes runs, batch records and eval records that
started before the cutoff, and prints what it freed; `--dry-run` lists them instead and
removes nothing, and `--keep N` spares the newest N runs whatever their age. It refuses to
run without `--older-than`. Records cite each other, so it works from the top down and
never breaks a reference: an eval it keeps keeps its batch and its judge's runs, a batch it keeps keeps every
run it made, a run it keeps keeps the run it `--continue`d from, and a batch whose
worktrees are still on disk (for a fresh task, one its record's `branch_made` says it made, or in a record without `ownership` one it did not fail on, before any attempt, because it was there already; for a task that ran in a slot, which outlives the batch, or
that was waiting for one: whose branch is still there and, its record's `branch_made` says, the task's own) stays with its runs, because `hrn batch rm` needs that record
to remove them (it says so, and names the command). A run with no result that wrote in
the last hour is taken to be still running and stays; a directory in `runs/` that is not
a run id is never touched. If any batch or eval record cannot be read, prune refuses:
that record may cite anything. Records go before the runs they cite, so a failure partway
never leaves a record pointing at nothing.

The freed size counts a linked original in full even when a kept run still holds it.

The one-hour activity rule lives in `internal/runlog/activity.go` and is shared by
prune and watch. It uses `events.jsonl`'s modification time, falling back to the run
directory when the transcript is absent. Watch displays an unfinished quiet run as
`stopped`; this adds no stored status or fields and leaves older records unchanged.
For an unfinished batch, watch considers the newest write to its record or any of
its referenced runs, including a run's result: an active first attempt keeps the
batch running even when the batch record itself is over an hour old, and a running
gate has the batch save its record again every ten minutes. See
[watch states](watch.md) for the display and Ada behaviour.

entries.key: docs/run-records.md > Run records > Ownership and execution flow
entries.content:
## Ownership and execution flow

Run records (`task.json`, `result.json`) and batch records carry an optional `owner`: who the
record belongs to, as `kind:value`. A local install writes `local:<OS user name>`, or
`$HRN_OWNER` when it holds a valid `local:`, `email:` or `user:` principal. Records written
before the field have none and belong to the local user, so nothing on disk is rewritten. Every
read that crosses an access boundary (the watch server, `hrn flow`) goes through one decision,
`owner.Viewer.CanReadRecord` (or `CanRead` without a directory): a record's owner reads
it, an admin grant reads all, and a project grant permits the named viewer to read
the named owner's records in that project. Anyone else is told the record does not
exist, so ids cannot be probed.

Project grants are a JSON list in `$HRN_HOME/grants.json` (default
`~/.hrn/grants.json`), for example:

```json
[{"viewer":"email:reader@example.com","owner":"local:me","project":"/absolute/path/to/repo"}]
```

`viewer` is an `email:` principal with a lowercase address or a `user:` principal.
`owner` is optional and defaults to the local owner; this also covers records written
before ownership. `project` is an absolute repository directory. A run's task
directory is resolved to its repository root by looking for `.git` in its parents
when available, falling back to the task directory. A batch uses `Result.Dir`.
The directory must equal the granted project or be below it after path cleaning,
with case ignored on Windows and a directory boundary required (`/repo2` is outside
`/repo`). Batch timelines check child runs independently; worktrees inside the
granted repository qualify, while runs outside it require their own access. The batch
record's own attempt summaries and gate output stay visible to anyone who may read
the batch.

hrn never writes the grants file. Public watch loads it at startup; absent means no
project grants, and malformed means no project grants plus one stderr error. Restart
watch after editing it. Local offline and LAN ownership behavior is unchanged.
Public record requests audit the requested id, decision and access basis in
`watch-access.log`; see [public watch](watch.md#behind-cloudflare-access).

A batch also appends its execution events to `batch-flows/<id>.jsonl`, one JSON object per
line. Each event has a version `v` (1), a sequence `seq` that continues when the file is reopened,
a time `t`, the `owner`, `batch`, `task`, `attempt` and `run` it concerns, a `step` id and its
`parent`, a `kind` (`batch`, `task`, `slot`, `attempt`, `route`, `decision`, `run`, `tool`, `gate`,
`commit`, `info`, `error`) and optionally a `status` (`started`, `waiting`, `ok`, `failed`,
`canceled`, `skipped`), `name`, `text`, `reason` and `next`. Later events for a step update it.
`reason` is only ever a recorded cause, such as a route row or a gate's exit; hrn never writes
model reasoning there. Text is masked for secrets and capped before it is written.

Step ids are fixed: `batch`, `task:<id>`, `task:<id>/slot`, `task:<id>/a<n>` for attempt n,
`task:<id>/a<n>/gate<k>`, and `<attempt>/run` for the attempt's run, whose tool calls are
`<attempt>/run/tool<n>`. A run outside a batch is `run:<id>`. Runs keep no flow file: their steps
are rebuilt from `events.jsonl` and the record (marked `derived`), and so is the flow of a batch
written before the file existed. A step whose parent is missing, such as a pruned run, is shown
as a gap rather than dropped. Readers skip a torn last line, duplicate sequence numbers and
versions newer than they know. Pruning a batch record removes its flow file too.
Prune also removes orphan `batch-flows/<id>.jsonl` files whose batch records are already
gone, regardless of age, and reports their count as `orphan_flows` (omitted when zero)
in `PruneResult` and in the command's text; `--dry-run` counts them without removing them.

entries.key: docs/run-records.md > Run records > Usage per turn
entries.content:
## Usage per turn

A `usage` event in `events.jsonl` is one model call's tokens, written when the backend
reports it, so a run's context can be followed turn by turn:

```json
{"t":"...","kind":"usage","usage":{"model":"claude-opus-5","input_tokens":5,"output_tokens":40,
 "cache_read_tokens":12000,"cache_write_tokens":30000,"context_tokens":42005}}
```

`context_tokens` is what that call carried: its input plus cache reads and writes. Zero
fields are left out. Which backends write them:

- **api**: one per request, as the response reports it.
- **claude**: one per main-loop assistant message. stream-json writes each content block of a
  message as a line of its own and repeats the message's usage on each, so hrn writes the
  event once per message id, after the message's last line, with the first line's figures
  and the largest output count of its lines (the count grows as the message is written).
  A sub-agent's messages fill its own context and are left out; they still count in the
  run's totals.
- **opencode**: one per step (`step_finish`).
- **codex** and **gemini**: none. Codex's `turn.completed` totals every model call of an
  agent turn and gemini reports the run's totals, so neither says what one call carried.

A `compaction` event is a compaction the backend reported: Claude Code's `compact_boundary`
line (from `compact_window`, or its own threshold). `text` says what set it off (`auto` or
`manual`) and `usage.context_tokens` holds the context just before it. No other backend
reports one. `hrn watch` and `hrn show --usage` also mark a turn whose context fell by more
than half from the turn before as a *probable* compaction; that is a reading of the
numbers, never written to the record.

Runs recorded before these events existed have none; the result's totals still hold.

entries.key: docs/run-records.md > Run records > Quota
entries.content:
## Quota

A `quota` event in `events.jsonl` is how much of the plan's quota the backend reported
used, numbers only:

```json
{"t":"...","kind":"quota","quota":{"five_hour":{"used_percent":38,"resets_at":1792600000},
 "week":{"used_percent":20,"resets_at":1793000000}}}
```

`used_percent` is 0 to 100 and `resets_at` is in Unix seconds; a window the report did not
carry is left out. Claude Code's `rate_limit_event` writes one: its
`rate_limit_info.unifiedWindows` (`five_hour`, `seven_day`, `utilization` 0 to 1), or, when
those are missing, the one window its `rateLimitType` names. No other backend writes one;
the watch Backends card and `hrn backends` read codex's quota from codex's own session files.

## The experience ledger

`$HRN_HOME/game/` (default `~/.hrn/game/`) holds:

- `events.jsonl`: one event per line, appended, never edited. A fold appends only
  keys the ledger lacks; when two folds meet, a repeated key is ignored when the
  ledger is read (the first line wins).
  Fields are `key` (source identity), `kind`, `track` (`delivery`, `practice`, `ada` or
  `badge`), `xp`, `at` and `repo` (GitHub owner/name, a folder name when no remote is
  set, or empty). Optional `cancels` names the key a correction takes back.
- `reps/<UTC date>.json`: daily exercise and named reads, including masked material,
  reveal and answer, answer time, attempt and self-mark.
- `settings.json`: optional `enabled` boolean. The game is on when the file or field
  is missing. `false` hides the scores; the ledger keeps recording.

This version writes these kinds:

| Kind | Key | XP | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `practice_rep` | `rep:<date>` | 30 | The daily exercise was answered. |
| `practice_read` | `read:<owner>/<repo>#<number>` | 20 | An answered read was merged afterwards. |
| `review_clean` | `review:<run id>` | 20 | A finished review ends `ok` with a non-empty final answer and no standalone word `blocking`. |
| `inside_ceiling` | `ceiling:<run id>` | 5 | A run ends `ok` with a timeout, or an api run has a cost ceiling and a known positive cost. |
| `routed_passed` | `routed:<run id>` | 10 | A routed run ends `ok` and, for a settled batch attempt, all its gates pass. |
| `routed_failed` | `routed:<run id>` | 0 | A routed batch attempt ends `ok` but its settled gates failed; it holds the key so the run never counts later. |
| `script_reused` | `script:<run id>/<name>` | 5 | A finished run calls a kept script, once per run and script. |
| `bug_squashed` | `batch:<batch id>/<task id>` | 15 | A task is no longer running, and a failed gate, apart from guards and infrastructure errors, is followed by an attempt with gates that all pass. |
| `first_use` | `first:batch`, `first:slot`, `first:eval`, `first:routed` | 25 | The earliest record of each feature, including a batch using a reusable slot. |
| `badge` | `badge:budget-keeper`, `badge:cheap-and-right`, `badge:veteran` | 0 | The twentieth run inside its ceiling, tenth routed pass, or delivery and practice experience reaching 5,000. |

An attempt is settled when its task is no longer running or a later attempt exists.
A routed run not yet recorded as an attempt waits while its worktree's task runs.
A syntax check (`bash -n`) is not a script reuse.

`at` is the run's end, the batch's start or the eval's start, in UTC. First-use
events use their source record's time; badges use the event that earned them.
Cancelled events are dropped before daily caps are applied, in order of `at`, then
`key`. Caps per kind and UTC date are four reviews, three bugs,
ten runs inside their ceiling, three routed passes and five script reuses.
Practice has a daily cap of one exercise and three reads. First uses and routed failures have no daily cap; badges remain once earned.

`hrn bot stats` folds every record on disk before it prints. `hrn runs prune` folds
every record on disk first and removes nothing if that or reading a run it would
remove fails; missing or malformed JSON run records have nothing to fold and may
be removed. When prune removes a batch whose task is still marked running, its
unfinished attempts are decided as failed first, even if all recorded gates passed.
`--dry-run` writes no ledger. Events whose records were pruned live
only in the ledger. See [Experience](experience.md) for the remaining design.

Batch task records can include `candidates` for best-of-k retries. Each entry
keeps the `brief_addition`, `run_id`, `gates`, total `tokens`, and `winner` flag
when present. The `branch`, `worktree`, `slot`, and `branch_made` fields record candidate ownership for cleanup. Entries are in proposal order. When a
winner is chosen but removing the original task's branch or worktree fails, a
last entry with no `brief_addition` or `run_id` keeps the original's claim so
`hrn batch rm` and `hrn gc` can still remove it.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces
entries.content:
# Reusable workspaces

[← README](../README.md)

An agent that needs a clean checkout usually runs `git worktree add` beside the
repository and rarely removes it, and each new folder builds its `target/` or
`node_modules/` from nothing. `hrn ws` keeps a fixed set of worktrees per repository
instead, called slots, and hands them out one at a time. A slot keeps its build output
from one task to the next.

```bash
cd "$(hrn ws take --branch fix-x)"   # a slot on branch fix-x; only its path goes to stdout
# ... work, commit, git push -u origin fix-x ...
hrn ws free                          # give it back (from anywhere inside the slot)
hrn ws list                          # who holds which slot, and what is in it
```

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > Slots and leases
entries.content:
## Slots and leases

Slots live at `<main checkout>/.hrn/slots/1`, `2`, and so on, whichever worktree of the
repository you run hrn from. hrn writes `.hrn/.gitignore` so they never show in the
repository's status. A slot is made on first use with `git worktree add --detach` and
then locked (`git worktree lock --reason "hrn ws slot"`), so `hrn gc` and
`git worktree prune` leave it alone. A bare repository has no checkout and is refused.
Takes add, list and lock slot worktrees one at a time, holding an OS file lock on
`.hrn/slots/.create.lock` while they do; a take waits up to two minutes for it. The
system releases the lock when its holder exits or crashes, so the file itself stays and
is harmless: it never needs deleting.
Git commands used by slot takes and batches can also inspect worktrees outside
that lock. If Git fails to read `.git/worktrees/<name>/commondir` while another
worktree is being created, hrn waits 250 ms and retries the command once. Other
errors, or a second failure, are returned as usual; cancellation stops the wait.
These commands use `LC_ALL=C` and an empty `LANGUAGE` so the retry recognises
Git's error text. Batch task creation (`worktree add -b`) is not retried: Git
may already have created the branch before failing to read another worktree.

Who holds a slot is a lease file beside it, `<n>.lease`:
`{"holder": "...", "taken": "...", "branch": "..."}`. It is created so that two callers
can never get the same slot. A lease held from the command line lasts until
`hrn ws free`. A lease that names a process (`"pid"`, which batch uses) is stale once
that process has exited, and the next take may take it over.
A process lease records its holder's start identity in `"start"` when available. On
Windows and Linux, a live process with the same id but another start does not hold it.
Leases written before `"start"` was added keep the old rule: a live pid holds the slot.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > Batches
entries.content:
## Batches

`hrn batch` takes the same slots, one per running task, unless its spec says
`"worktrees": "fresh"` (see [Slots or fresh worktrees](batches.md#slots-or-fresh-worktrees)).
Its lease names the task (`batch <id> task <task>`) and hrn's pid, so a crash leaves a
stale lease rather than a held slot. A batch never waits on a session: a slot
held by `hrn ws take` (no pid) among the ones it would try is passed over and it tries the
next number instead, up to the bound on its own slots (`parallel`, at least 5,
capped at 10). It waits on
slots other batches or its own running tasks hold, and on a lease it cannot read (see
[Batches](batches.md#slots-or-fresh-worktrees)). The task's branch `hrn/<id>` is made from the batch's
base and checked out in the slot. When the task ends, the slot is detached at the base
and its lease removed without asking for a push, because the work is meant to stay on
that local branch for `hrn batch merge`. A slot left with files in it keeps its lease
until hrn exits. A slot whose HEAD commits are on a local branch or tag is not skipped,
since a switch strands nothing there.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > Take
entries.content:
## Take

`hrn ws take` walks slots 1 to `--max` (default 5, at most 10 per repository)
and leases the first one that has no lease and nothing in it:

- A slot whose folder holds changes or untracked files, or whose HEAD has commits that
  a switch would strand (on no remote, local branch or tag), is skipped and named on
  stderr. hrn never cleans or
  resets someone's files. Ignored files (build output) are never
  touched.
- `--branch NAME` checks out the local branch of that name, or origin's branch of that
  name, tracked. If neither exists, it makes a new branch from the base. Git refuses a
  branch that is checked out in another worktree; hrn shows git's message and releases
  the lease.
- Without `--branch`, the slot is detached at the base.
- The base is `--base REF`, or origin's default branch, fetched first. With `--no-fetch`
  it is `origin/HEAD` as already fetched; if the clone has no `origin/HEAD`, take refuses
  rather than guess, and asks for `--base` or a fetch. A repository without an origin
  uses the main checkout's `HEAD`.

`--for TEXT` is the holder written into the lease (default `hrn ws take`). When every
slot up to `--max` is taken or skipped, take fails and names each slot, its holder and
since when, or why it was skipped.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > Free
entries.content:
## Free

`hrn ws free [PATH]` (default: the current folder) gives back the slot PATH is in. It
refuses while the slot holds changes or untracked files, and names the first few. It
also refuses while HEAD has commits that are on no remote, and says how many. In a
repository without remotes it checks for commits that are on no branch or tag instead.
It refuses a lease that names a process still running (a batch task's), which gives the
slot back itself. Otherwise it detaches HEAD where it is, so the branch is free for other checkouts and
for `hrn gc`, and removes the lease. The folder and its build output stay for the next
take.

An empty orphan branch has no commits to keep. Free detaches such a slot at the
main checkout's HEAD and removes its lease.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > A slot a batch kept
entries.content:
## A slot a batch kept

When a batch task ends with files in its slot, or with a commit on no branch, the slot
is not given back (`slot <n> kept` in the task's error). Free refuses it as it stands:
the work is on no remote, and a batch's work sits on a local branch by design. To get
the slot back:

1. Find it. `hrn ws list` shows it `taken` while hrn runs and `stale` once hrn has
   exited, with the holder `batch <id> task <task>`. If it is still `taken`, wait for
   the batch to end: free refuses a lease whose process is running.
2. Look at what is in it: `git -C <slot> status --ignored` and `git -C <slot> log`.
   Plain `git status` hides ignored files, and free does not look at them either; but
   checking out another commit overwrites an ignored file wherever that commit tracks the
   same path, in step 4 or at the slot's next take. Copy out any ignored file you value now.
3. Keep the work on a branch. Commit what you want to keep (`git -C <slot> add ...`,
   `git -C <slot> commit`), or remove what you don't. If HEAD is on the task's branch
   `hrn/<id>`, the commits are kept there. If HEAD is detached, name the commits:
   `git -C <slot> branch <name>`.
4. With any remote, whatever its name: detach the slot at a commit a remote-tracking
   branch holds. Free counts a commit at HEAD as unpushed when no remote-tracking branch
   holds it, and a local branch does not change that, so it would still refuse. Use the
   remote's default branch: `git -C <slot> switch --detach origin/main`, or
   `upstream/main` when the remote is `upstream`. `git -C <slot> branch -r` lists the
   remote-tracking branches; `git -C <slot> remote show <remote>` names the default.
   If `branch -r` shows no branch of that remote, it was never fetched: run
   `git -C <slot> fetch <remote>` first, then detach at `<remote>/<default>`. Only with no remote at all: skip this step. Free then counts only the commits at HEAD
   that no local branch or tag holds, and step 3 left none, so HEAD can stay where it is.
5. `hrn ws free <slot>`. It detaches HEAD where it is and removes the lease; the work stays
   on its branch. Merge or push the branch that now holds the work yourself, from the
   repository: `git merge <name>` when step 3 made a branch for detached commits,
   `git merge hrn/<id>` when the work was committed on the task's branch. `hrn batch merge`
   merges only tasks whose status is `pass`, even when you name them, and a task whose slot
   was kept usually is not (a failed commit ends as `error`). Use `hrn batch merge` only
   when `hrn batch show` reports the task passed.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > List
entries.content:
## List

`hrn ws list [--json]` prints one row per slot folder or lease: the number, the path,
`free`, `taken` or `stale`, the holder, since when, the branch (or the detached commit),
and `clean` or what is in it. A lease without a folder and a folder without a lease
both show.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > Issue leases
entries.content:
## Issue leases

`hrn run --issue REF`, the MCP `run` tool's `issue` and a batch task's `issue` lease a GitHub
issue to one run, so two runs never work on the same issue. REF is `owner/name#N`,
`https://github.com/owner/name/issues/N`, or `#N` (or `N`) for the repository of the
workspace's `origin` remote. Owner and name are lower-cased, as GitHub ignores their case.

entries.key: docs/workspaces.md > Reusable workspaces > Issue leases (part 2)
entries.content: GitHub issue to one run, so two runs never work on the same issue. REF is `owner/name#N`, `https://github.com/owner/name/issues/N`, or `#N` (or `N`) for the repository of the workspace's `origin` remote. Owner and name are lower-cased, as GitHub ignores their case. - **Where.** `~/.hrn/leases/issues/<owner>__<name>__<N>.lease` (under `$HRN_HOME` when set), so every checkout of the repository on this computer sees the same lease. The file is a slot lease with `issue`, `run` (the run id, or `<batch id>/<task id>`), `backend`, once known, `pr`, and `retired` while a Released comment is owed. It is taken after the run record exists and before the agent starts. - **Refusal.** A lease held by a live process refuses the take, even one of the same `hrn mcp` server: two runs are two holders. `hrn run` exits 2 and the MCP tool returns a tool error, naming the holder, its run, backend, branch and age; the run record is closed as an error. `--take-over` (`take_over` in a spec or MCP call) replaces the holder and notes whom. A lease whose process exited, or whose process id now names another process (the same start identity check as slots), is stale and taken over by the next take. - **GitHub.** A take also asks GitHub through `gh`: an open pull request whose closing references or body (`Fixes #N`, `closes: owner/name#N`, the issue's URL, with any of close/closes/closed/fix/fixes/fixed/resolve/resolves/resolved) close the issue, other than one from the run's own branch, refuses it like a live holder; so does a live claim comment by another worker. A claim is the first line ``Claim: <worker> on branch `<branch>` ``, and a later `Released: <worker>` closes it. Only comments by the account gh is logged in as count: every worker posts as that account, and anyone can comment on a public issue. It is stale after 24 hours when its branch has had no commit in 24 hours or does not exist. When the issue is free hrn adds the `claimed` label (created if missing) and comments ``Claim: hrn <run> (<backend>) on branch `<branch>` ``, plus `Takes over from <holder>.` on a takeover. These formats are shared with a claim tool outside hrn. A bare mention of the issue never holds it. - **Replaced holders.** When a take replaces a lease (its process ended, its pull request is merged or closed, or `--take-over`), the replaced worker's claim does not hold the issue: hrn comments, when that claim is open, `Released: <old worker>`, a blank line and why (`its process ended`, `pull request <url> is merged or closed`, `taken over by <worker>`). A dead or closed holder is released as soon as the claims are read, even if the take is then refused; a live holder only after hrn's own claim. A takeover releases other workers' live claims the same way. A Released comment that fails is owed: its worker goes into the new lease's `retired` list, the run's release posts it first (`retired by <worker>`) and keeps the lease if it fails again, and a take that replaces the lease releases those workers too. A refused take that owes one puts the replaced lease back. - **Two claims at once.** After commenting, hrn reads the claims again; the oldest open claim that is not stale or replaced wins. If that is another worker's, hrn comments `Released: <worker>`, a blank line and `claimed at the same time as <winner>`, gives the local lease back and refuses the take naming the winner. If that comment fails, the lease stays until the process ends, so the next take releases the claim. - **gh failing** (not installed, not logged in, not a GitHub repository) keeps the local lease and prints `GitHub claim skipped: <reason>`; the run goes on. With no branch (a detached `HEAD`, or not a git checkout) hrn keeps the local lease and prints `GitHub claim skipped: no branch (detached HEAD or not a git checkout)`; a branch with a backtick or a control character, which the Claim line cannot carry, is skipped the same way. Either way a replaced dead holder's release is owed, since its claim may be open. - **Release.** When the run (or batch task) ends, an open pull request from its branch keeps the issue: the lease is rewritten without a process and with `pr` set, so it outlives hrn. When gh finds none and hrn claimed the issue, it comments `Released: <worker>`, a blank line and the reason (`run <id> ended`), then removes the lease and the label when no other claim is open; if that comment fails the lease stays for the next take to release.
